steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening at dusk, Marion climbed the 127 steps.

She had counted them on her first night, twenty-three years ago, when her hands still shook from the ferry ride over and her boots were still clean. She counted them still, out of habit more than necessity. Some rituals outlive their reasons.

The lighthouse sat on a tongue of rock called Cutter's Point, a name that told you everything you needed to know about the water surrounding it. The sea here didn't forgive. It didn't even hesitate.

Marion had found this out about herself too.

On the night of the worst storm she could remember — the one they'd later name Eleanor, though no one asked her opinion — she had kept the light burning for eleven hours while the generator coughed and the windows flexed inward like something breathing. In the morning, she found a fishing boat anchored in the small cove below, its crew of four asleep in their cabin. They never knew she was there. They never came up to say thank you.

That was fine.

She hadn't chosen this life for the conversation.

Her daughter called on Sundays, asking when she was coming back to the mainland. Marion would stand at the window watching the water change color — green to grey to something with no name — and say *soon*, which both of them understood to mean *never*.

The lighthouse board had sent letters. Automation, they said. Progress. One man in an office could monitor seventeen lights at once with the right software. Marion had read the letters carefully and placed them in the stove.

More letters came. She burned those too.

Eventually, a young man arrived by boat with a clipboard and an apologetic expression. He stood in her kitchen drinking her tea and explaining, gently, that the light would continue to function — she didn't need to worry about that — it would simply no longer require a *keeper*.

Marion looked out at the water.

"There was a ship in 1987," she said. "The Resolute. The automated light at Brennan Point failed during the storm that November. Eleven men."

The young man looked at his clipboard.

"Our systems now have redundancies —"

"There was a boy in 1999," she continued. "Kayaking. Lost in the fog. He followed my light to the cove. He was fourteen years old."

The young man left. More letters came.

She burned those too.

On the last official night of her tenure — a date the board had set without her — Marion climbed the 127 steps as always. She lit the lamp. She sat in her chair by the window with a cup of tea and watched the beam sweep out across the black water in its steady, ancient rhythm.

*One. Two. Three. Dark.*

*One. Two. Three. Dark.*

Somewhere out there, a vessel was reading that pulse like a heartbeat, taking its bearing, adjusting course by degrees. The sailors wouldn't know her name. They wouldn't know about the letters or the young man with the clipboard or the 127 steps.

They would only know that the light was on.

Which was, Marion thought, finishing her tea, exactly enough.

She climbed back down in the dark, one hand on the rail, counting backwards from 127. When she reached the bottom, she put the kettle on for morning and slept without dreaming.

The light kept turning.
